A one-session seminar · Hebrew Bible and the Persian age

Chronicles: History Rewritten, and the Work of Sara Japhet

What the biblical books of Chronicles are, how their author worked, what Sara Japhet and other scholars have argued, and how much of the book can be called history

Prepared by Scholar · 16 November 2026

One session · about two hours · six parts

This seminar covers the biblical books of Chronicles (in Hebrew, Divrei ha-Yamim) in a single sitting. It reads the work as a piece of history-writing from the Persian or early Hellenistic age (roughly the fifth to the third century BCE). It gives the scholarship of Sara Japhet (1934–2024) the central place and sets it beside the other major voices in the field. The approach is historical and literary. It is not devotional.

Every page of the seminar follows the same rules. Each specific fact (a date, a title, a year of publication, a verse number) was checked against at least one source that does not depend on Wikipedia, or it is marked [unconfirmed] in the text. Quotations were copied from texts I actually opened, and the page number is given where the text has one. Where scholars disagree, the page names the scholars and does not choose for you.

Session plan (about 110 minutes)

2. Sources and method20Read four passages side by side with Samuel and Kings
3. Sara Japhet20Her life, her books and her main arguments

How claims are tagged

  • confirmed Checked in a primary record, or in two sources that do not depend on each other. Wikipedia did not count.
  • disputed Scholars disagree. The page names them.
  • unsupported No source I opened supports the claim. It appears only so that it can be set aside.
  • estimate A number or date that is rounded, calculated or approximate.
  • [unconfirmed] I could not check the point against an independent source.

Hebrew verse texts come from Sefaria (the Hebrew is “Miqra according to the Masorah”; the English is the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917, which is in the public domain). Japhet’s commentary is cited by the printed page numbers of the 1993 edition. In the side-by-side tables, this color marks words that differ between the two books and this color marks a clause that both books keep.

The short answer

What it is. Chronicles retells the history of Israel from Adam to the edict of Cyrus. It leans heavily on Samuel and Kings and changes them on purpose [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. confirmed

What Japhet argued. One author wrote Chronicles, and that author did not write Ezra–Nehemiah. The book is a general account of how divine justice governs history, and it was written “at the end of the fourth century BCE” [Japhet 1993, pp. 4, 7, 28]. disputed

What is still open. The date (the proposals span over four hundred years), the number of authors, the Hebrew text the author copied from, and how much of the book reports real events [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. disputed

Why it matters. It is the only full “second telling” of Israel’s monarchy inside the Hebrew Bible. Comparing it with Samuel and Kings shows how a community in the Persian province of Judah rewrote its own past.

Three corrections to common statements

  • Wellhausen’s title. His book of 1878 was called Geschichte Israels, Band I. The title Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels belongs to the second edition of 1883, and the English translation of 1885 uses it [Encyclopedia.com]. confirmed
  • The “one author” idea is older than Noth. Leopold Zunz proposed in 1832 that the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah, and F. C. Movers reached the same view in 1834 [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. Martin Noth’s work came in 1943 and built on a view already standard. confirmed
  • Publication details differ between sources. Japhet’s 1968 article runs pp. 330–371 in the JSTOR header and pp. 332–72 in her own bibliography. Her Hebrew book is dated 1977 by the Hebrew University and 1978 by Eisenbrauns. See the full list at the end.

1Part one

What Chronicles is

Name · canon · contents · time range · about 10 minutes

1.1 The name

The Hebrew title is דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים, Divrei ha-Yamim, “the events (or the words) of the days.” The title names a kind of book, a chronicle. The Hebrew Bible uses the same phrase for royal records that no longer exist: “the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel” (1 Kings 14:19), “of the Kings of Judah” (1 Kings 14:29), “of the Kings of Media and Persia” (Esther 10:2), and “the chronicles of King David” (1 Chr 27:24) [Japhet 1993, p. 1] [I Kings.14.19 on Sefaria] [I Kings.14.29 on Sefaria] [Esther.10.2 on Sefaria] [I Chronicles.27.24 on Sefaria]. confirmed

The book does not name itself. Japhet reports that the earliest attested names are in rabbinic sources (the Mishnah, the Talmud and the Midrash), and that the rabbis also called it “the Book of Genealogies” (Pesaḥim 62b) [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed for the verse checks above; the rabbinic citations rest on Japhet alone [unconfirmed].

The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) titles the book Paraleipomena, “things left over” or “omitted.” Japhet observes that this title describes what the translators thought the book contained, not its genre, and that it “may carry negative connotations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. Jerome preferred chronikon, and “it is probably through Jerome’s suggestion and influence that ‘Chronicles’ was taken up by most modern translations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed on Japhet’s authority; I did not open Jerome’s prologue [unconfirmed].

1.2 Its place in the canon

The canon is the list of books a community treats as authoritative. The Hebrew Bible has three divisions: Torah, Prophets and Writings (Ketuvim). Chronicles sits in the Writings, but its position there varies:

  • A Talmudic baraitha (a teaching from the early rabbinic period) lists Chronicles last among the Writings (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b). Most manuscripts and printed editions follow that order [Japhet 1993, p. 2].
  • Two of the oldest and best Masoretic manuscripts, the Leningrad Codex and the Aleppo Codex, place it first among the Writings, and the Masoretic notes follow the same order [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. The Aleppo scan on Wikimedia Commons is labeled “Ketuvim 1 – Chronicles” [Commons file description]. confirmed
  • The standard scholarly editions of the Hebrew Bible (Biblia Hebraica Kittel and Stuttgartensia), which print the Leningrad text, move Chronicles to the end, “succumbing to the more dominant Babylonian tradition” [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. confirmed

Japhet adds that “either of the two locations … may be well justified”: as a comprehensive history of the people, Chronicles can open the Writings or close them [Japhet 1993, p. 2].

1.3 Contents

Japhet divides the book into three parts that differ in content, in literary form and in emphasis [Japhet 1993, p. 8]:

  1. 1 Chr 1–9, an introduction made of genealogies and lists. It runs from Adam to the twelve sons of Jacob, then through the tribes, and ends with the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
  2. 1 Chr 10 – 2 Chr 9, the history of Israel under David and then Solomon. David’s part has four sub-units, Solomon’s three [Japhet 1993, p. 10].
  3. 2 Chr 10–36, the history of the kingdom of Judah from the break with the northern tribes.

Figure 3 shows how the 1,765 verses divide. Sefaria’s Masoretic verse numbering gives 943 verses in 1 Chronicles and 822 in 2 Chronicles [1 Chr on Sefaria] [2 Chr on Sefaria]. confirmed estimate for the verse counts per part, which I added up from the chapter lengths in that numbering. The second bar uses the figure of 558 verses with a “recognized, known parallel” in Samuel or Kings [Endres et al., via arXiv, section 4.1]. disputed: counts of “parallel” verses vary with the rules used, and I saw only the citing paper, not the 1998 synopsis [unconfirmed].

1.4 The time range

Chronicles describes Israel’s history “from beginning to ‘beginning’ — from the inception of human existence with Adam, through the destruction of the first commonwealth during the reign of Zedekiah, to the new commencement with the declaration of Cyrus” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. The book ends with that declaration (2 Chr 36:22–23). The edict is dated to the first year of Cyrus, and Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE according to the British Museum’s catalog entry for the Cyrus Cylinder [British Museum] [2 Chr 36:22–23 on Sefaria]. confirmed

The narrated time (Adam to Cyrus) is a different thing from the time of writing. The book was composed long after the last events it tells. Part 4 sets out the proposed dates.

Key dates
  1. 539 BCECyrus takes Babylon; the edict in 2 Chr 36:22–23 is dated to his first year.
  2. 6th–2nd c. BCERange of proposed dates of writing, over four hundred years (Welch to the Maccabean period); the most common view is the fourth century (Japhet, p. 24; Part 4).
  3. 1832Zunz: the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah.
  4. 1968Japhet reopens the question of common authorship.
  5. 1993Japhet’s commentary, still the standard English work.
Why it matters

Chronicles is the last major biblical history in time of writing, yet it covers the earliest events. Because it sits at the end of a long chain of earlier books, it shows how those books were read by the first people to treat them as a library.

2Part two

Sources and method

Four passages side by side · named sources · the text behind Samuel · about 20 minutes

2.1 The Chronicler’s library

The author of Chronicles is anonymous, and scholars call him “the Chronicler.” Japhet describes his working method this way: “Because of his peculiar literary method of employing and citing earlier works, the ‘library’ which was available to the Chronicler may be easily reconstructed” [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. That library includes the whole Pentateuch, the books of Samuel and Kings (which scholars call the Deuteronomistic history, a long history of Israel shaped by the outlook of the book of Deuteronomy), and also Zechariah, Lamentations, and two passages taken from Ezra–Nehemiah: the edict of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1–3a) and a list of the inhabitants of Jerusalem (Neh 11:3–19) [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. confirmed on Japhet’s authority; I checked the Cyrus passages in the text myself (Table 1, below).

Most of what Chronicles shares with another book it shares with Samuel and Kings. Japhet calls this the “synoptic” nature of the book: much of it “represents a literal citation of earlier biblical” text [Japhet 1993, p. 28]. Her own description of the technique, from her note on 2 Chronicles 32, is worth keeping in mind for every table below: the Chronicler uses “the Deuteronomistic story of Kings as his point of departure on the one hand, and the extensive reworking through omissions, additions, rephrasing and epitomization on the other” [Japhet 1993, p. 976]. confirmed

Wherefore the LORD brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, who took Manasseh with hooks, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. What the differences mean has been argued for 150 years. Here are the main readings.

A. The census (2 Sam 24:1 and 1 Chr 21:1)

  • Wellhausen (1878; English 1885) lists the change as one of many “improving touches”: instead of “the anger of Jehovah was kindled against Israel, and he moved David,” Chronicles has “Satan stood up against Israel and moved David” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. He also notes that David pays “600 shekels of gold” where Samuel has “50 shekels of silver”: “to make the king pay right royally costs the Chronicler nothing” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. confirmed for what he wrote.
  • Japhet reads the change differently. She grants that the Chronicler removed God’s anger and gave the incitement to “another agent,” so that “David himself is presented as exclusively responsible” [Japhet 1993, p. 373]. But she doubts that satan here is a proper name. The word has no article, and in the Hebrew Bible a common noun becomes a proper name by taking the article; so she reads it as “an adversary” and calls the anonymous figure “the antithesis of Joab,” who tries to dissuade David [Japhet 1993, pp. 374–376]. She also notes that nowhere else in Chronicles does an independent power of evil appear [Japhet 1993, p. 375]. disputed: most English translations print “Satan” [Japhet 1993, p. 374], and Japhet argues against that reading.

B. Bathsheba (2 Sam 11 – 12 and 1 Chr 20:1)

Chronicles keeps the sentence “But David tarried at Jerusalem,” but the story that sentence introduces in Samuel is gone. Wellhausen’s explanation: the Chronicler omits what “does not contribute much to the glorification of the king,” and the result in 1 Chr 20:1 is “meaningless” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 178]. Japhet agrees that the text is incoherent, and she traces the cause to method: “A strict adherence to the original text and at the same time its adaptation according to various tendencies may result in internal incoherence” [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. She also reports that Rudolph restored a missing passage by conjecture, and she explains why that repair is weak [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. confirmed for the quotations; whether the omission is theological or accidental is disputed.

C. The promise to David (2 Sam 7:16 and 1 Chr 17:14)

In Samuel, David’s own house and kingdom will be secure. In Chronicles the subject changes: “it is not the ‘house’ and ‘kingdom’ of David which ‘shall be established’; rather, Solomon will be confirmed for ever in the ‘house’ and ‘kingdom’ of the Lord” [Japhet 1993, pp. 334–335]. Japhet ties this to the problem that David did not build the Temple, which the Chronicler met in three ways: by enlarging David’s role in preparing the Temple, by softening David’s ideal image, and by stressing that Solomon is also “chosen” [Japhet 1993, p. 335]. Wellhausen read the same verse and found the original meaning “volatilised into an abstract idealism” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 177]. confirmed for the quotations; the interpretation is disputed.

D. Manasseh (2 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33)

The two accounts of Manasseh’s sins (2 Kgs 21:1–9 and 2 Chr 33:1–9) are close in wording. They part at the end: Kings gives the king a short closing notice and burial “in the garden of Uzza,” and Chronicles inserts an Assyrian capture, a prayer, and a return to Jerusalem (33:11–13). Wellhausen: “The Book of Kings knows no worse ruler than Manasseh was; yet he reigned undisturbed for fifty-five years … This is a stone of stumbling that Chronicles must remove” [Wellhausen 1885, pp. 206–207]. Japhet argues that the whole of this period was reworked “to provide … more solid theological cohesiveness,” beginning “in the change of Manasseh’s figure,” and she shows how the change prepares the new account of Josiah [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019, 1034]. confirmed for the quotations; whether the captivity happened is disputed (Part 4).

Hebrew and English for all eight passages in Table 1 were fetched from Sefaria and compared with the verse numbers cited by Japhet and Wellhausen. The 1917 translation renders “moved” where the Hebrew verb is wayyaset (“incited”); Japhet translates it “incited” [Japhet 1993, p. 373].

2.3 The sources the Chronicler names

Samuel and Kings end most reigns with a note such as “the rest of the acts of … are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.” Chronicles keeps the habit but changes the titles. Japhet counts eighteen works cited in the closing formulas: six with general titles (for example “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel”) and twelve ascribed to prophets (for example “the chronicles of Samuel the seer”), including Samuel, Nathan, Gad, Ahijah, Iddo, Shemaiah, Jehu, Isaiah and Hozai [Japhet 1993, p. 20]. confirmed

Whether these were really eighteen separate books is disputed. Japhet notes that a work with a general title is never cited together with a prophetic work for the same reign, and that two double titles (“the chronicles of Jehu son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel,” 2 Chr 20:34; “the vision of Isaiah … in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” 2 Chr 32:32) show that the prophetic works were “extracts from a comprehensive book” [Japhet 1993, p. 20]. Wellhausen went further. He accepted Ewald’s view that the “Midrash of the Book of Kings” (2 Chr 24:27) is the real title of the source called simply “the Book of Kings,” and concluded that “in Chronicles we find ourselves fully within the period of the scribes” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 227]. [2 Chr 24:27 on Sefaria]

2.4 Which text of Samuel did he copy?

A Vorlage (German for “model” or “source text”) is the exact wording an author or translator worked from. The question is whether the Samuel-Kings in front of the Chronicler matched our Masoretic Text (MT, the medieval Hebrew text). It sometimes did not.

  • Japhet reports that where Chronicles differs from MT Samuel, it sometimes agrees with variant readings of the Septuagint, and that fragments of Samuel from Qumran (4QSama) show matches with Chronicles against MT. She cites W. E. Lemke’s 1965 article (Harvard Theological Review 58, pp. 349–363) and Eugene Ulrich’s study of the Qumran text of Samuel (1978) [Japhet 1993, p. 29] [Lemke 1965]. She concludes that Chronicles reflects “a Vorlage different from the MT” [Japhet 1993, p. 29]. confirmed
  • S. L. McKenzie (1985) pressed the idea further: he argued that the Chronicler’s version of the Deuteronomistic history was not the form we have. Japhet disagrees: she holds that the history was “extant basically in its final canonical form” and that the Chronicler consciously departs from it [Japhet 1993, p. 27] [McKenzie 1985]. disputed
  • Japhet shows how to test a case. The omission of 2 Sam 5:4–5 in 1 Chr 11 was long thought to be the Chronicler’s choice. 4QSama also lacks the verses, which raises the chance that they were missing from his copy. But she finds the same verse (2 Sam 5:5) reused in 1 Chr 3:4 without the phrase “over Judah,” and concludes the omission is the Chronicler’s own work [Japhet 1993, p. 238]. confirmed for her argument; whether she is right is still disputed.

Japhet’s caution on method: “the more familiar we become with the Chronicler’s literary methods, historical views and theology, the more refined our considerations may become” [Japhet 1993, p. 19].

Why it matters

A difference between Chronicles and Kings can mean three different things: the Chronicler changed the text; the Chronicler copied a different text of Samuel-Kings; or the Masoretic Text changed later. Telling these apart is the main skill of the field, and the Qumran scrolls made it possible.

Life · works · main arguments · about 20 minutes

3.3 Her main arguments

The commentary of 1993 holds her mature view in one place. Quotations below are from its Introduction, by the printed page numbers.

1. Two books, two authors

“Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah constitute two different works by two different authors. Not only do they illustrate an array of small and large differences — in language, style, literary method, etc. — and express different and often opposite views about central issues of biblical history and theology, but when considered in their totality they represent two varieties of biblical historical writing during the Persian-Hellenistic period” [Japhet 1993, p. 4]. confirmed for the quotation; the conclusion is disputed. Gunneweg, Haran, Blenkinsopp, Ackroyd and Pohlmann restated the older view in new forms [Japhet 1993, pp. 3–4].

2. One book, one author

Against the many attempts to cut Chronicles into layers (Part 4), she holds that “it is one work, composed essentially by a single author, with a very distinct and peculiar literary method.” She allows later changes “in particular in the lists, which are most susceptible to change,” and doubts that “a rational, meticulous harmony of all the possible details was ever aimed at by the Chronicler” [Japhet 1993, p. 7]. confirmed for the quotations; disputed as a position.

3. No single narrow purpose

Wellhausen, Torrey, Noth, Rudolph and Freedman each found one aim: to answer the Priestly Code, to fight the Samaritans, or to support the house of David under Zerubbabel [Japhet 1993, p. 43]. Japhet doubts that one aim could explain “such an enormous enterprise.” In her words, Chronicles “is not a manifesto devoted to a specific political movement but a more general and comprehensive theological stock-taking, striving to achieve a new religious balance in the face of a changing world” [Japhet 1993, pp. 43–44]. confirmed for the quotation; disputed as a position.

4. Justice that is immediate and individual

The book’s “theory of ‘reward and punishment’” shows history as “a concrete manifestation of divine justice.” In her summary: “Reward is mandatory, immediate and individual. Every generation is requited for its own deeds, both good and evil, with no postponement of recompense; there is no accumulated sin and no accumulated merit.” Two things attend this: warning and repentance. “Man is always offered a chance to repent” [Japhet 1993, pp. 44–45]. The Manasseh story (Part 2, case D) is her example of how the Chronicler adjusted older history to fit this rule [Japhet 1993, p. 1019]. confirmed for the quotations.

5. “Great Israel,” the land and the king

She finds a view of “‘great Israel’ in the broadest sense,” settled across the whole land from the beginning, with “no Gentiles in the land of Israel” in the Chronicler’s picture; the exodus and the exile are “muted” [Japhet 1993, pp. 46–47]. David and Solomon appear “in a much more positive light than in earlier biblical historiography,” yet “neither of them can be considered perfect or ‘ideal’” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. confirmed for the quotations.

6. Lists as proof

The many lists give the account “the validity and authority of ‘accurate fact’.” A modern reader “may find some lists more authentic than others,” but that does not change their literary job [Japhet 1993, p. 41]. Her caution on sources: even if sources existed, “even authentic sources may be used in an uncritical or anachronistic manner,” so reliability must be judged “on a case-by-case basis” [Japhet 1993, pp. 18–19]. confirmed for the quotations.

7. The date

Japhet puts the book “at the end of the fourth century BCE.” Her grounds: the language is Late Biblical Hebrew; there is no sign of Greek influence; and the Persian administrative system of Ezra–Nehemiah is missing, which may point to a non-Persian setting [Japhet 1993, pp. 25–26]. Her count from the line of Jehoiachin (1 Chr 3:17–24) gives a window of roughly 460–320 BCE, though she calls that method “problematical” [Japhet 1993, p. 26]. See Figure 7. disputed

Why it matters

Japhet changed the question. Earlier scholars asked what older documents lay beneath Chronicles and what political cause it served. She asked what the book itself is: one work with its own method, its own view of history and its own place beside Ezra–Nehemiah. Even readers who reject her answers now have to argue with them.

4Part four

The debates

Authorship · date · how far Chronicles is history · about 25 minutes

Chronicles has been read in three main ways over 150 years: as late and unreliable history (Wellhausen), as a work with many hands (Noth and others), and as one author’s unified answer to his times (Japhet and many later writers). This part follows the three disputes in turn: who wrote it, when, and how far it can be trusted.

4.1 Authorship and layers

Two questions are tangled together. The first: did one person write Chronicles and also Ezra–Nehemiah? The tradition said yes, and said that person was Ezra the scribe (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a; also John of Salisbury and Ralph Niger in the Middle Ages) [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. Zunz (1832) and Movers (1834) kept the idea of one author but dropped Ezra and called him “the Chronicler”; their view “eventually gained general recognition” [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. confirmed Albright alone, among modern scholars, went back to Ezra himself [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. confirmed After 1968 the view of two independent works spread [Japhet 1993, p. 4].

The second question is whether the book as we have it is the original. Its mix of narrative and long lists, of priestly and Deuteronomistic features, led many to see layers. Japhet sorts the attempts into four groups: “source” theories (Kittel, Benzinger); the removal of whole sections such as the lists (Welch); tradition-history with “wild growth” around a core close to the Deuteronomistic history (Noth, Rudolph, Willi); and staged composition (Galling; Cross, with three stages from the sixth to the fourth century) [Japhet 1993, pp. 5–6]. Her own verdict: “each of these approaches has come with its own, idiosyncratic ‘Chronicler’” [Japhet 1993, p. 7]. confirmed for what she says; the disputes themselves are disputed.

Cross and Freedman: a political reading

Freedman (1961) and Cross (1975), with others, tied the book to the time of Zerubbabel, the leader from the house of David in the late sixth century [Japhet 1993, pp. 7, 25] [Cross 1975]. Freedman argued that its purpose was to support the claims of the house of David to rule, and in particular its claim to authority over the Temple and its worship [Japhet 1993, p. 43]. Japhet doubts that any single political aim fits the book (Part 3, argument 3). disputed

4.2 The date

Nothing in Chronicles names an event of its own time, so every date is an inference. Japhet lists the clues [Japhet 1993, pp. 24–26]:

  • The Hebrew is Late Biblical Hebrew: not earlier than the post-exilic age.
  • No Greek influence is visible, which suggests a time before the strong Hellenistic influence of the third century BCE.
  • The line of Jehoiachin in 1 Chr 3:17–24 reaches “between seven and fourteen generations” after him, depending on how the damaged list is read; at about twenty years a generation this gives a wide window.

Wellhausen placed Chronicles “fully three hundred years” after the Books of Samuel and Kings, “after the downfall of the Persian empire” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 172]. A recent commentator, Knoppers, reaches “around the mid third century BCE,” by allowing time both for Chronicles to be quoted by later writers and for its own sources to become authoritative, as reported by one reviewer [ABR review of Knoppers]. disputed: I did not read Knoppers myself, so the figure rests on the review [unconfirmed]. Japhet’s own text says the most common view puts the book in the fourth century or toward its end, and that the full range of proposals spans over four hundred years [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. confirmed

Why it matters

The date decides what the book is evidence for. Written around 400 BCE, it speaks about the Persian province of Judah. Written in the third century, it speaks about a community already under Hellenistic rule. Either way it is a witness to its own age first, and to the age of David second.

4.3 How far is Chronicles history?

Japhet separates two questions that older scholars joined: whether the Chronicler had sources, and whether his book is reliable. She holds that he did use sources beyond Samuel and Kings, because “the analysis of Chronicles as a literary work seems to leave no doubt” of it, and that this still does not settle reliability: “even the existence of ‘sources’ does not guarantee the reliability of the book” [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. Even Wellhausen granted non-synoptic sources [Japhet 1993, p. 19]. confirmed

Wellhausen’s own verdict was harsher. Of the long list of David’s supporters in 1 Chr 12 he wrote that the “vast numbers … are not matters of indifference here, but the principal thing,” and he called the whole picture “hardly credible” [Wellhausen 1885, pp. 174–175]. Japhet’s answer is about purpose, not accuracy: lists serve to bolster the account with “accurate fact” [Japhet 1993, p. 41]. Both are disputed as readings. Three test cases follow.

Case 1. Hezekiah’s tunnel

Kings and Chronicles both mention Hezekiah’s water works, with different words (Table 2). Kings speaks of the pool, the conduit and bringing water “into the city.” Chronicles says he “stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon” and brought them “straight down on the west side of the city of David” [2 Kgs 20:20 on Sefaria] [2 Chr 32:30 on Sefaria].

Table 2. Hezekiah’s water works in Kings and in Chronicles. Hebrew: Sefaria; English: JPS 1917.

2 Kings 20:202 Chronicles 32:30
2 Kings 20:20

וְיֶתֶר דִּבְרֵי חִזְקִיָּהוּ וְכׇל־גְּבוּרָתוֹ וַאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אֶת־הַבְּרֵכָה וְאֶת־הַתְּעָלָה וַיָּבֵא אֶת־הַמַּיִם הָעִירָה הֲלֹא־הֵם כְּתוּבִים עַל־סֵפֶר דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים לְמַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה׃

Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

2 Chronicles 32:30

וְהוּא יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ סָתַם אֶת־מוֹצָא מֵימֵי גִיחוֹן הָעֶלְיוֹן וַיַּישְּׁרֵם לְמַטָּה־מַּעְרָבָה לְעִיר דָּוִיד וַיַּצְלַח יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ בְּכׇל־מַעֲשֵׂהוּ׃

This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

  • The Siloam Tunnel is 533 meters long. It is usually called Hezekiah’s Tunnel, and, according to Maeir and Chadwick, most scholars accept it as part of his preparations before the Assyrian attack of 701 BCE [Maeir and Chadwick 2013].
  • In 2003 Frumkin, Shimron and Rosenbaum reported radiocarbon and uranium–thorium dates that, they wrote, prove an Iron Age II date and show that “the Biblical text presents an accurate historic record” of the tunnel’s construction [Frumkin et al. 2003]. disputed: this is their conclusion, and the abstract is all I read.
  • Other studies disagree. Sneh, Shalev and Weinberger (2010) argue that the tunnel is later and was cut by Manasseh; they read 2 Chr 32:30 as pointing to a different channel, the Siloam Channel. Reich and Shukron (2011) argue that the tunnel was dug before Hezekiah. Maeir and Chadwick criticize the first view: Isaiah 7:3 and 8:6 point to the older channel being in use before Hezekiah, and Hezekiah’s revolt left four years for the work (705 to 701 BCE) [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. disputed
  • No inscription names Hezekiah as the builder [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. The tunnel therefore tests the verse; the verse does not prove the date.

Case 2. Manasseh in Assyrian records

Kings gives Manasseh a short closing notice; Chronicles adds a capture, a prayer, and a return (2 Chr 33:11–13; Table 1, part D). The Assyrian text called Esarhaddon’s Prism B lists “Manasseh, king of Judah” among twelve rulers of the Levant who were called on, in 676/675 BCE, to send building materials for a monument at Nineveh [Esarhaddon Prism B]. That is the only Assyrian mention of him I opened, and it says nothing about a captivity, for or against. A silence of this kind is weak evidence; the prism is a list of contributions. disputed Japhet argues from the book’s theology, not from outside records: the story of Manasseh’s repentance fits the rule that every generation is paid for its own deeds, and it prepares the new Josiah story [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019, 1034]. I did not find a source that settles the question.

Case 3. Yehud: how big and how populous?

Yehud is the Aramaic name for Judah as a province of the Persian empire. The genealogies and lists of Chronicles have been used as a map of the province, so its size matters. Finkelstein (2010) argues that the distribution of stamped jar handles with the name Yehud covers only the area around Jerusalem (between Ramat Rahel and the City of David), with some finds at Jericho and En-Gedi. The list of wall builders in Nehemiah 3, in his view, does not fit Persian-period archaeology, and he suggests it may reflect the Hasmonean period of the second century BCE. From site sizes he estimates about 61 built-up hectares and “ca. 12,000 people” for the whole province, about half the figure of Carter and Lipschits (20,000 to 30,000), and a few hundred in Jerusalem itself [Finkelstein 2010]. disputed: Finkelstein’s numbers rest on a density assumption of 200 persons per built-up hectare, which he sets lower than other scholars do. estimate

For Chronicles the result is two-sided. On one hand, a small province is hard to square with the “great Israel” of the genealogies. On the other, Finkelstein says that the genealogies of Judah and Benjamin “cannot help reconstructing the ‘territoriality’ of Yehud,” as J. W. Wright had tried to do in 2006, because “they may represent post-Persian-period realities” [Finkelstein 2010, n. 27]. disputed

Another test: the capture of Jerusalem

Kalimi (2005), as summarized by his reviewer, concludes that Chronicles “does not contain authentic data about the capture of Jerusalem”: it leaves out the earlier attempts at the city, and adds “all Israel” in 1 Chr 11:4 against 2 Sam 5:6. Its aim is to mark a new epoch with David’s reign [ABR review of Kalimi]. disputed: I know this only from the review.

Why it matters

The disputes are not signs of a weak field. Each answer changes what the book can be used for: as evidence of what happened under the kings, as evidence of what the Persian-age community believed, or both. Learn to ask, for any claim about Chronicles, which of those two uses it assumes.

5Part five

Why it matters

A rewritten past · the Second Temple setting · reception · about 15 minutes

5.1 A history rewritten, on purpose

Chronicles “constitutes a comprehensive parallel to the earlier biblical historiography from Genesis to Kings” and ends “pointing toward a new era” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. It is not a copy. The Chronicler used Samuel and Kings “as his point of departure,” and reworked them “through omissions, additions, rephrasing and epitomization” [Japhet 1993, p. 976]. Three results are worth keeping in mind.

  • A different David. The Bathsheba story is gone, David’s sins are reduced to two, and he is ruled out of building the Temple because “he shed blood” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. His son Solomon is “flawless” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. confirmed
  • A different Josiah. In Kings the great reform begins in his eighteenth year, after the book of the Law is found. In Chronicles “Josiah did not wait until the eighteenth year of his reign. The change of disposition occurred in the eighth year of his reign ‘while he was yet a boy’ (34.3)”; the reform cleans the land, not the Temple, and the finding of the book comes by chance during repairs [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019–1020]. Japhet explains these changes as answers to theological problems in the older account: Josiah is praised lavishly in Kings, yet in that account he ruled seventeen years amid idolatry unpunished [Japhet 1993, p. 1019]; and the judgment on Judah stays fixed whatever Josiah did, which leaves “no possibility of repentance” [Japhet 1993, p. 1034]. confirmed for the quotations.
  • Continuity with the Temple. Kalimi (2005), as summarized by his reviewer, argues that the Chronicler stresses continuity between the First and Second Temples. He follows the tradition in Jeremiah 27–28 and Ezra that the Temple vessels were kept by the Babylonians, where 2 Kings 24:13 says they were destroyed [ABR review of Kalimi]. disputed: I know this only from the review.

5.2 The Second Temple setting

The world behind the book is the Persian empire and, after it, the Hellenistic kingdoms. In that world Judah was a small province. Figure 10 shows the empire; Figure 12 shows a coin of the province itself.

The book ends with a decree of Cyrus. The clay cylinder in Figure 11 is the best-known royal text of his reign. The British Museum’s account says it was “written from a purely Babylonian point of view,” that Cyrus appears in it as the chosen servant of Marduk, and that it records the return of deported peoples and their gods to their cities. The same entry states that the cylinder “says nothing of human rights” (against a popular label), and that “the return of the Jews and of other deported peoples was a significant reversal of the policies of earlier Assyrian and Babylonian kings” [British Museum]. The museum’s list of names in the inscription has no Jerusalem and no Judah. The cylinder therefore matches the kind of policy that Ezra and Chronicles attribute to Cyrus, and it does not confirm the edict as the Bible words it. confirmed for what the museum says; disputed for how much the cylinder supports the biblical edict.

Table 3. The edict of Cyrus, as Chronicles ends and as Ezra begins. The two texts are the same through “which is in Judah” and then divide. Differences and kept clauses are marked.

2 Chronicles 36:22–23 (the end of the book)Ezra 1:1–3 (the same edict, continued)
2 Chronicles 36:22–23

וּבִשְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס לִכְלוֹת דְּבַר־יְהֹוָה בְּפִי יִרְמְיָהוּ הֵעִיר יְהֹוָה אֶת־רוּחַ כּוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ־פָּרַס וַיַּעֲבֶר־קוֹל בְּכׇל־מַלְכוּתוֹ וְגַם־בְּמִכְתָּב לֵאמֹר׃ כֹּה־אָמַר כּוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס כׇּל־מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהוּא־פָקַד עָלַי לִבְנוֹת־לוֹ בַיִת בִּירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה מִי־בָכֶם מִכׇּל־עַמּוֹ יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ וְיָעַל׃

Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying: ’Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia: All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD, the God of heaven, given me; and He hath charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whosoever there is among you of all His people—the LORD his God be with him—let him go up.’

Ezra 1:1–3

וּבִשְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס לִכְלוֹת דְּבַר־יְהֹוָה מִפִּי יִרְמְיָה הֵעִיר יְהֹוָה אֶת־רוּחַ כֹּרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ־פָּרַס וַיַּעֲבֶר־קוֹל בְּכׇל־מַלְכוּתוֹ וְגַם־בְּמִכְתָּב לֵאמֹר׃ כֹּה אָמַר כֹּרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס כֹּל מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמָיִם וְהוּא־פָקַד עָלַי לִבְנוֹת־לוֹ בַיִת בִּירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה׃ מִי־בָכֶם מִכׇּל־עַמּוֹ יְהִי אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ וְיַעַל לִירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה וְיִבֶן אֶת־בֵּית יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלִָם׃

NOW IN the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying: ’Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia: All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD, the God of heaven, given me; and He hath charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whosoever there is among you of all His people—his God be with him—let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel, He is the God who is in Jerusalem.

Chronicles stops at “let him go up” (Hebrew וְיָעַל, we-ya‘al); Ezra goes on, “to Jerusalem … and build the house of the LORD.” Kalimi reads the cut as deliberate, a call to more exiles to return, since the last word of Chronicles is “go up” [ABR review of Kalimi]. Others see an ordinary ending of the book. disputed: Japhet notes only that the edict is one of two passages Chronicles takes from Ezra–Nehemiah [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. The point for the seminar is the reuse itself: the book that retells the monarchy ends on a text from the Persian age and from another biblical book. This is also why the question of common authorship (Part 4) matters.

Money confirms that the province had its own identity. Finkelstein notes the “high level of silver” in the Yehud coins and links it with their role in the Temple economy, but he says this only “seemingly” [Finkelstein 2010]. disputed

Why it matters

Chronicles belongs to the age of the Second Temple. It shows no trace of the Persian administrative system (Japhet, p. 26), yet its themes (a central Temple, a Levitical order, one people in one land, justice in each generation) answer the needs of a small community led from Jerusalem under a distant empire. To read it is to see how that community told its own past.

5.3 How the book was received

In Jewish tradition

  • It was counted as part of the canon from early times. Josephus’s “thirteen books” of prophetic history “must have included Chronicles” (Japhet’s inference), and the rabbis list it among the Writings [Japhet 1993, pp. 1–2]. confirmed
  • It was studied less than other books. Walfish writes that “Chronicles has not traditionally been a very popular book for Jews to study,” that “there is no midrashic compilation on Chronicles,” and that there are only nineteen extant medieval commentaries up to the end of the eighteenth century, “a very low figure” [Walfish 2012, pp. 101–102]. confirmed
  • Yet it was never ignored. Walfish also says that Kalimi shows it “was never totally neglected,” and that a circle of scholars in twelfth-century Germany took a particular interest in it; one anonymous commentary of that school, long attributed to Rashi, is dated by Viezel to 1155 [Walfish 2012, pp. 103–104, 106]. Radak (David Kimhi), a grammarian and exegete of Provence, wrote one of the best-known commentaries [Walfish 2012, p. 102]. confirmed
  • Spinoza (1670), in a passage Walfish quotes, wrote that he had “always been astonished” that certain books were included in the Bible while others were excluded, and added “it is not my intention to detract from their authority.” Walfish reads the passage as about Chronicles and says Spinoza “distinctly states that he is not out to question the book’s authority” [Walfish 2012, p. 104].

In Christian tradition

  • The Septuagint (Greek) title Paraleipomena, “things left over,” “may carry negative connotations,” and some Syriac fathers wanted the book removed from scripture; “except for these late voices … the canonicity of Chronicles is firmly established in all traditions” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed
  • The Septuagint and Vulgate place it after Kings, an order that “influenced its position in many modern translations” [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. In the Middle Ages Christian writers such as John of Salisbury and Ralph Niger, and Stephen Langton (who wrote a commentary on Chronicles), took it as the work of Ezra [Japhet 1993, pp. 3, 24]. confirmed
  • The claim that Chronicles was “neglected” by Christian readers as a rule: no source I opened shows it. The sources show doubts in one Syriac school and a late rise of critical doubt, not general neglect. unsupported

In modern research

Wellhausen’s verdict set the tone for a century: late, partial, unreliable. From the 1960s onward the book’s own method and message came to the front (Freedman, Willi, Williamson, Japhet). Japhet’s Ideology is credited by its publisher with being “recognized as a major distillation of the themes underlying the ideology of the book of Chronicles” [Japhet, Ideology]. confirmed for the quotation; the judgment is the publisher’s.

Key dates
  1. End of the narrativeChronicles tells the fall of Judah under Zedekiah, then turns to the edict of Cyrus (Japhet, p. 8).
  2. 539 BCECyrus takes Babylon; the Cyrus Cylinder was written after this.
  3. c. 375–332 BCESilver “YHD” coins of the province of Yehud (dating from the Commons description).
  4. c. 460–320 BCEWindow for the last generation in Jehoiachin’s line (Japhet’s count).
  5. 2nd c. BCEHellenistic and Maccabean age; the latest date proposed for Chronicles.

6Part six

Discussion

Eight questions with collapsible answers · about 20 minutes

Use these eight questions in a group of four to ten. Spend about two minutes on each before opening the answer. The answers give reasons and sources, not a single correct view.

Question 1. The Greek title Paraleipomena means “things left over.” What does the title assume about the book, and why does Japhet think it does not describe the book well?

It assumes that Chronicles is a supplement to Samuel and Kings. Japhet notes that the title names “what the translators regarded as its contents,” not its genre, and that it “may carry negative connotations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. The Hebrew title, “events of the days,” names a kind of writing (a chronicle) [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. Question for the group: does a supplement still tell a different story from the one it supplements? Table 1 suggests that it does.

Question 2. In 2 Sam 24:1 the anger of the LORD moves David to count the people; in 1 Chr 21:1 “Satan” does. What are two ways to read the change?

(a) The Chronicler removed God’s anger and gave the act to another agent, so that David “is presented as exclusively responsible” [Japhet 1993, p. 373]; Wellhausen listed it among many “improving touches” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. (b) Japhet doubts that satan is a proper name, because it has no article; she reads “an adversary,” “the antithesis of Joab” [Japhet 1993, pp. 374–376]. The group may ask what each reading assumes about the Chronicler’s view of evil. disputed

Question 3. 1 Chr 20:1 keeps “But David tarried at Jerusalem,” though the story it introduces is gone. What does this show about the Chronicler’s method?

That he copies large pieces of text and cuts others, and that the join can fail. Wellhausen calls the result “meaningless” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 178]. Japhet: “A strict adherence to the original text and at the same time its adaptation according to various tendencies may result in internal incoherence” [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. Both agree the text is awkward; they differ on what the awkwardness proves.

Question 4. Did the author of Chronicles also write Ezra–Nehemiah? List two arguments for each side.

Yes: Zunz found it hard to give all of Ezra–Nehemiah to Ezra, and so gave both books to the Chronicler; later scholars restated the view in new forms, and Haran (1986) wrote on “the identical lines at the end of Chronicles and beginning of Ezra,” the plainest clue (Table 3) [Japhet 1993, pp. 3–4]. No: Japhet points to differences “in language, style, literary method,” and to “different and often opposite views about central issues of biblical history and theology” [Japhet 1993, p. 4]; Kalimi gives linguistic and other differences [ABR review of Kalimi]. Remember the second question, layers in the book itself, is separate (Figure 6). disputed

Question 5. Why is the date of Chronicles so hard to fix, and what does each proposed date change about how you read the book?

The book names no event of its own time, so every date is an inference from language, from the absence of Greek influence, and from the genealogy of Jehoiachin [Japhet 1993, pp. 24–26]. A date near 400 BCE makes it evidence for Persian-period Judah; a date near 250 BCE (Knoppers, as reported [ABR review of Knoppers]) makes it evidence for an early Hellenistic community. Figure 7 shows the spread. disputed

Question 6. Hezekiah’s tunnel, Manasseh in Esarhaddon’s list and Finkelstein’s estimate for Yehud: what can each test, and what can it not?

The tunnel can test whether 2 Chr 32:30 points to a real work and when it was built, but the studies disagree (Table 2; Case 1) [Frumkin et al. 2003] [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. Esarhaddon’s list shows that Manasseh was an Assyrian vassal, but is silent about a captivity [Esarhaddon Prism B]. Finkelstein’s survey-based numbers limit the size of the province and so test the “great Israel” of the lists, but they depend on a density figure he chooses [Finkelstein 2010]. None of the three settles the book’s reliability as a whole. disputed

Question 7. Chronicles ends in mid-sentence with “let him go up.” What are two readings of that ending?

Kalimi reads it as a deliberate call for more exiles to return [ABR review of Kalimi]. A plainer reading is that the Chronicler quoted only as much of the edict as he needed to close the history on a note of new beginning, which fits Japhet’s description of the book as running “from beginning to ‘beginning’” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. Table 3 puts the two texts side by side. disputed

Question 8. How should a historian use a book like Chronicles?

Two uses are possible: as evidence for the time it describes (the kings), and as evidence for the time it was written (the Persian or early Hellenistic community). Japhet insists that these be kept apart: sources, reliability and theology are “different considerations” [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. Wellhausen judged that in Chronicles “we find ourselves fully within the period of the scribes” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 227], which is to use the book mainly in the second way. A sound habit: for each claim, say which use it assumes, and what outside evidence, if any, can be set beside it.

Glossary

Achaemenid empire
The Persian empire founded by Cyrus. It ruled Judah from 539 BCE until the Greek conquest (see the map in Part 5).
Canon
The list of books a community treats as authoritative.
Chronicler
The anonymous author of Chronicles, as scholars call him. Whether he was one person is part of the debate.
Deuteronomistic history
The books Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, seen as one history shaped by the outlook of Deuteronomy.
Genealogy
A list of descent. 1 Chr 1–9 is almost all genealogy.
Hellenistic period
The age of Greek rule and influence after Alexander the Great (late fourth century BCE onward).
Iron Age II
The archaeological period roughly from 1000 to 586 BCE, the time of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
Late Biblical Hebrew
The form of biblical Hebrew used in the Persian period and after, with features that differ from earlier books.
Masoretic Text (MT)
The standard medieval Hebrew text of the Bible, edited by the Masoretes (scribes who fixed the vowels, accents and notes).
Paraleipomena
The Greek title of Chronicles, “things left over.”
Qumran, 4QSama
A scroll of Samuel from the caves at Qumran, near the Dead Sea. Its text sometimes agrees with Chronicles against the Masoretic Text.
Septuagint
The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.
Synoptic
“Seen together”: passages that run in parallel and can be set side by side, like Table 1.
Theodicy
An account of how a just God allows the evils of history.
Tradition history
A method that studies how texts grew by stages through repeated use and revision.
Vorlage
The exact text an author or translator worked from.
Writings (Ketuvim)
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah and the Prophets. Chronicles is in it.
Yehud
The Aramaic name for Judah as a province of the Persian empire.
Yehud stamp impressions
Seal impressions on jar handles bearing the name “Yehud”; their spread is used to outline the province.

Corrections and points I could not confirm

These are the places where sources disagree or where I stopped short of a confirmation.

Corrected
  • Wellhausen’s book of 1878 is Geschichte Israels I; Prolegomena is the title from 1883, and the English translation of 1885 uses it [Encyclopedia.com].
  • The “one author” idea is not Noth’s: Zunz (1832) and Movers (1834) came first [Japhet 1993, p. 3].
  • “Christian neglect” of Chronicles: not supported by anything I opened; the book was in every canon after the late Syriac doubts [Japhet 1993, p. 1].
Sources disagree
  • Japhet’s 1968 article: pp. 330–371 (JSTOR) or 332–72 (Japhet herself).
  • Ideology in Hebrew: 1977 (Hebrew University) or 1978 (Eisenbrauns); the English reprint: 2004 or 2009.
  • Her presidency of the World Union of Jewish Studies: 2006–2009 (Hebrew University) or 2005–2009 (IIAS).
  • Her commentary’s page count: 1,077 or 1,007, so none is given.
  • Knoppers’s date: “around the mid third century” in one review; I did not read the commentary.
  • Place of her birth: Tel Aviv in one record; no second source found.
Not confirmed
  • 558 parallel verses: from a 2025 paper citing a 1998 synopsis that I did not see [Endres et al., via arXiv].
  • Hebrew commentary on Chronicles, 2024: known from a publisher listing and from a notice that it was “in the press” [Am Oved listing].
  • The page range of Japhet’s 1985 article in JSOT 33.
  • Jerome’s prologue and the rabbinic references to the book’s names: through Japhet only.
  • Cross’s dates for his three stages: I have only Japhet’s summary, “sixth century” to the “fifth and fourth” [Japhet 1993, p. 6].
  • Whether Williamson, Willi, Noth and others held Ezra–Nehemiah to be by a different or the same author: Japhet’s survey does not say for each.
  • Yairah Amit’s position, and the arguments of Klein and Ben Zvi: no source opened.
  • The exact day of Japhet’s death in March 2024.
